column1: # Cases for require-absolute-rm.sh — one per line: <verdict><TAB><command>
# verdict is `pass` (hook exits 0) or `block` (hook exits 2). Use \n for a
# newline inside a command; the runner decodes it with printf %b.
# These live in a file rather than an inline shell loop for a structural reason:
# a test suite for a deletion guard is full of deletion commands, and passing
# them as arguments to an inline function trips the guard on the test run
# itself. Reading them from disk keeps the command line clean.
# --- absolute targets are the whole point ---
# --- relative targets, the failure this hook exists for ---
# --- nested shells: the text is on the command line, so it is read ---
# --- left alone by design: committed code establishes its own root ---
# --- heredoc bodies are data, not commands ---

column2: git commit -F - <<'EOF'\nMentions `rm` and `xargs rm` in prose.\nEOF
cat > /tmp/doc.md <<EOF\nUse rm carefully; rm -rf build is bad.\nEOF
